Recurrent Networks (RNN, LSTM, GRU)

A recurrent neural network reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a hidden state, a vector that summarises what it has read so far, from each step to the next. LSTM and GRU cells add learned gates that decide what to keep, write and erase in that state, so that information and gradients survive over much longer sequences.

1Overview

Why it matters

Recurrent networks are a classic way to give a neural model a memory of what came earlier in an ordered input: speech arriving from a microphone, words typed on a keyboard, the daily demand for a product, the moves in a game. They process one step at a time with a fixed-size state, so the cost per step does not grow with the history. That is why they are still found where a model must stream its output, fit on a phone, or act several times a second. The examples in this lesson include on-device speech recognition and keyboard prediction at Google, demand forecasting on AWS, and a Dota 2 agent.

The second reason to learn them is diagnostic. A plain RNN fails in one characteristic way: the gradient that should teach it about an early input is multiplied by a factor at every step on the way back, so it shrinks to nothing or blows up. Gates, gradient clipping, truncated backpropagation and residual connections in deep stacks are all ways of coping with that problem or its cost, and it is part of the background to why attention-based models later took over most language work (see Attention and Transformers). Anyone who debugs a sequence model, reads speech or time-series code, or must choose an architecture needs this mechanism.

Before you start

  • Training Deep Networks (Optimizers, Dropout, Normalization)Intermediate

What you will be able to do

  • Unroll a recurrent network over a short sequence and compute its hidden states by hand.
  • Explain backpropagation through time, including why the gradient of a shared weight is a sum over time steps.
  • Show with numbers why gradients vanish or explode over long sequences, and apply gradient clipping and truncated backpropagation.
  • Trace one LSTM step and one GRU step, saying what each gate does to the state.
  • Choose between a plain RNN, an LSTM, a GRU and a non-recurrent model for a sequence task, and justify the choice.

Key terms

Hidden state
A vector the network carries from one time step to the next. It is the network's summary of the input read so far and the only memory a plain RNN has.
Time step
One position in the sequence, such as a word, an audio frame or a day's sales figure. The recurrent cell is applied once per time step.
Unrolling
Drawing the recurrent network as a chain with one copy of the cell per time step. All copies share the same weights.
Backpropagation through time (BPTT)
Ordinary backpropagation applied to the unrolled chain. The gradient of each shared weight is the sum of its contributions from every time step.
Truncated BPTT
A variant that stops the backward pass after a fixed number of steps, such as 16, while still carrying the hidden state forward.
Vanishing gradient
The training signal for early time steps shrinks towards zero because it is multiplied by a factor below 1 at each step going back, so long-range effects are not learned.
Exploding gradient
The opposite failure. The factor is above 1, the gradient grows exponentially and one update can throw the weights far away or produce NaN values.
Gradient clipping
Rescaling the whole gradient vector when its norm exceeds a threshold, so that a single bad step cannot move the weights too far.
Gate
A vector of numbers between 0 and 1, computed by the network with a sigmoid, that is multiplied elementwise with another vector to let a fraction of it through.
Cell state
The extra memory vector of an LSTM. It is updated by scaling and addition rather than by repeated squashing, which gives gradients a more direct route back through time.

2Explanation

Introduction

A feed-forward network, such as the ones in Neural Network Fundamentals, takes an input of fixed size and returns an output. Much real data is neither fixed in size nor made of independent pieces. A sentence has a different number of words each time, and what a word means depends on the words before it. A model that reads such data needs a way to remember what it has already seen.

A recurrent neural network (RNN) does this with one extra vector. It reads the sequence one time step at a time, where a step is a word, an audio frame or a day's sales figure. At each step it combines the new input with its hidden state, a vector of numbers summarising everything read so far, and produces a new hidden state. The same weights are used at every step, so one small network can read a sequence of any length. An everyday analogy is reading a page while keeping a running summary in your head: after each sentence you update the summary instead of re-reading the page.

Drawing one copy of the network per time step makes the idea visible. This is called unrolling, and it turns the loop into a long chain that ordinary backpropagation can handle.

The chain is also where the trouble starts. To learn that an early input mattered, the training signal must travel backwards through every step in between, and at each step it is multiplied by a factor. Over a few steps that is harmless. Over fifty it usually leaves almost nothing, or an enormous number. LSTM (long short-term memory) and GRU (gated recurrent unit) cells give that signal a safer route by using gates: numbers between 0 and 1, computed by the network itself, that decide how much of the old state to keep and how much new information to write.

This lesson builds the plain RNN first, then the training algorithm (backpropagation through time), then the vanishing and exploding gradient problem with a hand-computed example, and then the LSTM and GRU cells. It assumes you know how training deep networks works, including the chain rule from backpropagation. The real-world examples cover translation, keyboard prediction, forecasting, speech recognition and a game-playing agent.

How it works

One step of a plain RNN

A plain (Elman) RNN keeps a hidden state hth_tht​ and updates it from the new input xtx_txt​ and the previous state:

ht=tanh⁡(Wih xt+Whh ht−1+b),h0=0h_t = \tanh(W_{ih}\,x_t + W_{hh}\,h_{t-1} + b), \qquad h_0 = 0ht​=tanh(Wih​xt​+Whh​ht−1​+b),h0​=0

WihW_{ih}Wih​ maps the input into the state, WhhW_{hh}Whh​ maps the old state into the new one, and bbb is a bias. PyTorch's nn.RNN (opens in a new tab) uses exactly this update, with two bias vectors that add up to one. The same WihW_{ih}Wih​, WhhW_{hh}Whh​ and bbb are used at every step, so the parameter count does not depend on the sequence length, and tanh keeps every entry of the state between -1 and 1. If you do not pass a start state, PyTorch uses zeros, as its nn.LSTM (opens in a new tab) page states.

What you do with the states depends on the task. To classify a whole sequence, feed only the last state to an output layer. For tagging or language modelling, feed every state to an output layer. For generation, feed each output back in as the next input. Karpathy's article on RNNs (opens in a new tab) lays out these input and output patterns and shows generation with character-level text models.

python
import torch
from torch import nn

lstm = nn.LSTM(input_size=64, hidden_size=128, batch_first=True)
x = torch.randn(32, 50, 64)      # (batch, time steps, features)
output, (h_n, c_n) = lstm(x)     # output: (32, 50, 128); h_n and c_n: (1, 32, 128)

Training: backpropagation through time

Unroll the loop over TTT steps and the network becomes an ordinary deep graph in which every layer reuses the same weights. Backpropagation through time (BPTT) is backpropagation on that graph. Write at=Wihxt+Whhht−1+ba_t = W_{ih}x_t + W_{hh}h_{t-1} + bat​=Wih​xt​+Whh​ht−1​+b for the pre-activation. The gradient moves back one step at a time:

∂L∂at=∂L∂ht⊙(1−ht2),∂L∂ht−1=Whh⊤ ∂L∂at\frac{\partial L}{\partial a_t} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_t} \odot (1 - h_t^{2}), \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_{t-1}} = W_{hh}^{\top}\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial a_t}∂at​∂L​=∂ht​∂L​⊙(1−ht2​),∂ht−1​∂L​=Whh⊤​∂at​∂L​

where ⊙\odot⊙ is elementwise multiplication, and a loss term at step ttt is added to ∂L/∂ht\partial L/\partial h_t∂L/∂ht​ if that step has its own output. Because WhhW_{hh}Whh​ is used at every step, its gradient is a sum with one term per step:

∂L∂Whh=∑t=1T∂L∂at ht−1⊤\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_{hh}} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\partial L}{\partial a_t}\, h_{t-1}^{\top}∂Whh​∂L​=t=1∑T​∂at​∂L​ht−1⊤​

Two costs follow. Memory grows with TTT, because every state is kept for the backward pass, and the backward pass is as sequential as the forward pass. For long sequences the usual remedy is truncated BPTT: cut the sequence into chunks of τ\tauτ steps, carry the hidden state across a chunk boundary as a plain value, and stop the gradient there. The Dive into Deep Learning chapter (opens in a new tab) reports that truncation works well in practice and biases training towards simpler, more stable models. In PyTorch you cut the graph with h = h.detach() between chunks.

Why long sequences are hard

For the loss at step TTT to teach the network that input xkx_kxk​ mattered, the gradient must travel from hTh_ThT​ back to hkh_khk​. By the chain rule that is a product of one Jacobian per step:

∂hT∂hk=∏t=k+1Tdiag⁡(1−ht2)  Whh\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_k} = \prod_{t=k+1}^{T} \operatorname{diag}(1 - h_t^{2})\; W_{hh}∂hk​∂hT​​=t=k+1∏T​diag(1−ht2​)Whh​

A product of T−kT-kT−k similar factors behaves like a number raised to the power T−kT-kT−k. Pascanu, Mikolov and Bengio (opens in a new tab) make this precise. Let γ\gammaγ bound the slope of the activation (1 for tanh, 1/4 for sigmoid). If the norm of WhhW_{hh}Whh​ (its largest singular value) is below 1/γ1/\gamma1/γ, every Jacobian in the product has norm below 1 and the long-term components of the gradient vanish exponentially fast; a norm above 1/γ1/\gamma1/γ is necessary for them to explode. The paper states these conditions with the largest eigenvalue, which is the same number when WhhW_{hh}Whh​ is symmetric.

The two failures look different. When the signal vanishes, the loss still falls, but the network learns only short-range patterns because nothing tells it that early inputs matter. When it explodes, one update can throw the weights far away, and the loss jumps or turns into NaN. Exploding gradients have a cheap fix, gradient clipping: if the norm ∥g∥\lVert g \rVert∥g∥ of the whole gradient exceeds a threshold θ\thetaθ, replace ggg by θ g/∥g∥\theta\, g / \lVert g \rVertθg/∥g∥. The direction is kept and the step is bounded. PyTorch's clip_grad_norm_ (opens in a new tab) computes one norm over all parameters, rescales the gradients in place and returns the norm from before clipping, which is worth logging. Vanishing gradients have no equally cheap fix, and they motivated gated cells.

LSTM: a memory updated by addition

An LSTM adds a second vector, the cell state ctc_tct​, and three gates. In PyTorch's notation, with σ\sigmaσ the sigmoid function (PyTorch keeps two bias vectors per gate; they are merged into one here):

it=σ(Wiixt+Whiht−1+bi)ft=σ(Wifxt+Whfht−1+bf)gt=tanh⁡(Wigxt+Whght−1+bg)ot=σ(Wioxt+Whoht−1+bo)ct=ft⊙ct−1+it⊙gtht=ot⊙tanh⁡(ct)\begin{aligned} i_t &= \sigma(W_{ii}x_t + W_{hi}h_{t-1} + b_i) \\ f_t &= \sigma(W_{if}x_t + W_{hf}h_{t-1} + b_f) \\ g_t &= \tanh(W_{ig}x_t + W_{hg}h_{t-1} + b_g) \\ o_t &= \sigma(W_{io}x_t + W_{ho}h_{t-1} + b_o) \\ c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g_t \\ h_t &= o_t \odot \tanh(c_t) \end{aligned}it​ft​gt​ot​ct​ht​​=σ(Wii​xt​+Whi​ht−1​+bi​)=σ(Wif​xt​+Whf​ht−1​+bf​)=tanh(Wig​xt​+Whg​ht−1​+bg​)=σ(Wio​xt​+Who​ht−1​+bo​)=ft​⊙ct−1​+it​⊙gt​=ot​⊙tanh(ct​)​

The forget gate ftf_tft​ scales the old cell state, the input gate iti_tit​ scales the new candidate gtg_tgt​, and the output gate oto_tot​ decides how much of the cell is shown to the rest of the network as hth_tht​.

This helps because the cell state is changed by scaling and adding, not by pushing it through a weight matrix and a tanh each step. Along the direct path, ∂ct/∂ct−1=diag⁡(ft)\partial c_t / \partial c_{t-1} = \operatorname{diag}(f_t)∂ct​/∂ct−1​=diag(ft​): no matrix, no tanh slope, only the forget gate. The gates also depend on ht−1h_{t-1}ht−1​, so weaker side paths exist, but if the network keeps forget gates near 1 for the units that must remember, the gradient across many steps is a product of numbers near 1. Olah's walkthrough (opens in a new tab) calls the cell state a conveyor belt for this reason. One practical detail: with zero biases a fresh gate outputs about 0.5, so a new LSTM starts by halving its memory each step. Keras's LSTM layer (opens in a new tab) therefore adds 1 to the forget-gate bias at initialisation by default (unit_forget_bias=True) and cites Jozefowicz et al. for the practice. Check what your framework does.

GRU: the same idea with fewer parts

The gated unit now called GRU was introduced by Cho et al. (opens in a new tab) in a paper on RNN encoder-decoders. It has no separate cell state and only two gates. In PyTorch's form:

rt=σ(Wirxt+Whrht−1+br)zt=σ(Wizxt+Whzht−1+bz)nt=tanh⁡(Winxt+bin+rt⊙(Whnht−1+bhn))ht=(1−zt)⊙nt+zt⊙ht−1\begin{aligned} r_t &= \sigma(W_{ir}x_t + W_{hr}h_{t-1} + b_r) \\ z_t &= \sigma(W_{iz}x_t + W_{hz}h_{t-1} + b_z) \\ n_t &= \tanh\big(W_{in}x_t + b_{in} + r_t \odot (W_{hn}h_{t-1} + b_{hn})\big) \\ h_t &= (1 - z_t) \odot n_t + z_t \odot h_{t-1} \end{aligned}rt​zt​nt​ht​​=σ(Wir​xt​+Whr​ht−1​+br​)=σ(Wiz​xt​+Whz​ht−1​+bz​)=tanh(Win​xt​+bin​+rt​⊙(Whn​ht−1​+bhn​))=(1−zt​)⊙nt​+zt​⊙ht−1​​

The update gate ztz_tzt​ blends old and new. Where ztz_tzt​ is near 1 the unit copies its old value forward and ignores the input; where it is near 0 the unit takes the candidate ntn_tnt​. The reset gate rtr_trt​ decides how much of the old state feeds the candidate, and near 0 the unit behaves as if it started fresh. PyTorch's nn.GRU (opens in a new tab) applies rtr_trt​ after the multiplication by WhnW_{hn}Whn​, which differs from the original paper and is done for efficiency. A GRU has three weight blocks per layer where an LSTM has four, so it is smaller and quicker, and the d2l chapter (opens in a new tab) notes that it often performs comparably.

Stacks, directions and cost

Layers can be stacked, with layer 2 reading layer 1's output sequence. Deep plain stacks train badly: the GNMT paper (opens in a new tab) reports that simple stacked LSTMs work well up to about 4 layers and very poorly beyond 8, and fixes this with residual connections. A bidirectional layer runs one RNN forward and one backward over the same sequence, which needs the whole sequence in advance and so rules out streaming. Finally, step ttt needs the result of step t−1t-1t−1, so time cannot be parallelised within one sequence, and information from kkk steps back passes through kkk updates. The Transformer paper (opens in a new tab) names that sequential nature as a limit on parallelism within a training example; see Attention and Transformers.

python
import math

wx, wh, b, y, xs = 1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 0.8, [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]

def loss(wx, wh, b):
    h = 0.0
    for x in xs:
        h = math.tanh(wx * x + wh * h + b)
    return 0.5 * (h - y) ** 2

hs = [0.0]                                    # forward pass
for x in xs:
    hs.append(math.tanh(wx * x + wh * hs[-1] + b))

dh, g = hs[-1] - y, {"wx": 0.0, "wh": 0.0, "b": 0.0}
for t in range(len(xs), 0, -1):               # backward pass
    da = dh * (1 - hs[t] ** 2)
    g["wx"] += da * xs[t - 1]
    g["wh"] += da * hs[t - 1]
    g["b"] += da
    dh = da * wh
print({k: round(v, 6) for k, v in g.items()})
eps = 1e-6
print(round((loss(wx + eps, wh, b) - loss(wx - eps, wh, b)) / (2 * eps), 6))

The first line printed is {'wx': -0.054699, 'wh': -0.41651, 'b': -0.915422} and the second is -0.054699.

Edge cases and limitations

A large recurrent weight can vanish faster instead of exploding
In the one-unit tanh example a recurrent weight of 1.5 does not give an exploding gradient. Once the state saturates near 0.86 the tanh slope 1 - h^2 is about 0.26, so the per-step factor is about 0.4 and the gradient shrinks faster than with a weight of 1.0 (exercise 1 measures 4e-22 against 3e-3 after 50 steps). Pascanu et al. give a recurrent matrix larger than 1/gamma (stated for its largest eigenvalue) as a necessary condition for explosion, not a sufficient one, so monitor the gradient norm during training instead of reasoning from the weights alone.
Gates reduce vanishing but do not remove it
A forget gate of 0.9 still leaves 0.9^50 = 0.005 of the signal after 50 steps, and a gate of 0.5 leaves about 1e-15. LSTMs and GRUs keep long-range gradients alive only where the network has learned to hold the gate near 1, and the cell can still be overwritten. Dependencies that span thousands of steps remain hard, which is one reason attention-based models replaced recurrence for language.
Padding changes what the last output means
To batch sequences of different lengths you pad the short ones. Reading the last time step of a padded batch returns the state after the padding for every sequence shorter than the longest, and the loss counts padded positions unless it is masked. Either pack the sequences or gather the output at each sequence's true last index, and mask the loss.
Truncation limits what gradients teach, not what the state carries
With truncated BPTT over 16 steps, as in OpenAI Five, the hidden state still flows across chunk boundaries while the agent plays, but no gradient flows back across them. The model can use information from further back only if short-range gradients taught it to store that information. A dependency longer than the truncation length is unlikely to be learned.
Feeding samples back compounds errors
When a recurrent model feeds its own samples back in, as the DeepAR paper does when forecasting, an early wrong sample changes every later state. AWS's documentation advises against prediction_length values above 400 because they make the model slow and less accurate (it does not name error build-up as the reason), and suggests aggregating the data to a coarser frequency to reach further into the future.
Bidirectional layers cannot stream
A bidirectional RNN needs the whole sequence before it can produce its first output, because the backward half starts at the end. Streaming systems such as the Gboard speech recognizer process audio as it arrives and cannot wait. Use bidirectional layers only when the full input is available, as in the bottom layer of the GNMT encoder.

When to use it, and when something simpler is enough

Use it when

  • Inputs arrive as a stream and a result is needed after every step, with memory and compute per step that do not grow with the history, as in speech recognition and keyboard prediction.
  • A small model must run on a phone or embedded device, where one gated layer with a few megabytes of weights is practical.
  • The task is sequential decision making under partial observability, where an agent must remember what it saw earlier.
  • You have many related series of moderate length and want one shared probabilistic forecaster.

Think twice when

  • Relationships span hundreds or thousands of positions and you have parallel hardware and enough data, because attention-based models give every pair of positions a short path.
  • The history that matters fits in a fixed window and you can build lag features, because a windowed model is simpler to train and debug.
  • You must train quickly on very long sequences, because recurrence cannot be parallelised over time within a sequence.

A simpler alternative. A sliding window of the last k values or words fed to a feed-forward network, a linear autoregressive model, or gradient-boosted trees on lag features is often enough and trains faster. Move to a recurrent model when the useful history length varies, when a window large enough to cover it makes the input too big, or when output must be produced as the data arrives.

Key takeaways

  • A recurrent network reuses one set of weights at every time step and passes a hidden state forward, so its memory is a fixed-size vector and its parameter count does not depend on sequence length.
  • Backpropagation through time is ordinary backpropagation on the unrolled chain, and the gradient of each shared weight is a sum with one term per time step.
  • The gradient reaching an early step is a product of one Jacobian per step, so it shrinks or grows exponentially with distance; in the worked example only about a billionth of the error signal reached the first input at length 30.
  • Gradient clipping bounds exploding updates and truncated BPTT limits cost, while the gates of LSTM and GRU address vanishing by giving the gradient a path built from scaling and addition.
  • An LSTM keeps a separate cell state controlled by forget, input and output gates, and a GRU drops the cell state and uses two gates, with three weight blocks against four; neither removes vanishing completely.
  • Choose recurrence for streaming, on-device and stateful-agent settings, and consider windowed models or attention when dependencies are long or training must be parallel.

3Real-world applications

5 documented uses of Recurrent Networks. Each one names the real system, the problem it solves and its tradeoff, with links to the sources.

  1. Google Neural Machine Translation: a deep LSTM encoder and decoder in Google Translate
  2. Gboard next-word prediction: a small CIFG recurrent model trained with federated learning
  3. Amazon SageMaker DeepAR: one recurrent forecaster shared across hundreds of related time series
  4. Gboard on-device speech recognition with an RNN transducer built from LSTM networks
  5. OpenAI Five: a 4096-unit LSTM as the memory of a Dota 2 agent

Example 1 of 5

Google Neural Machine Translation: a deep LSTM encoder and decoder in Google Translate

GoogleDocumented in a paper

The GNMT paper by Wu et al. (2016) describes the translation system that Google announced in September 2016, and a Google Research post from the same month announces its production launch for Chinese to English in Google Translate. The model is an encoder-decoder built from stacked LSTM layers. [13][14][15]

The problem

Translation has to read a source sentence of any length, keep what matters about it, and write a target sentence of a different length one word piece at a time. The previous production approach, phrase-based translation, worked on words and phrases that were translated largely separately. The new system had to use the whole sentence as context, learn from data end to end, and still be cheap enough to serve interactively.

Where this topic fits

Recurrent networks are the whole model here. An LSTM encoder turns the source sentence into one vector per position, an LSTM decoder produces the target one piece at a time, and gated cells plus residual connections keep an 8-layer stack trainable.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. The source text is split into wordpieces, a limited set of common sub-word units, so a rare word becomes a short sequence of pieces the model has seen.
  2. The encoder is a stack of 8 LSTM layers. Only the bottom layer reads the sentence in both directions; the other seven run left to right, which keeps more of the computation parallel.
  3. Between layers, starting from the third layer from the bottom, each LSTM's output is added to its input (a residual connection), so the gradient has a short path back through the stack as well as the long path through every layer.
  4. The decoder is also an 8-layer LSTM stack. In an encoder-decoder of this kind, each step takes the previously produced piece and the decoder's own state, consults the encoder outputs through attention, and predicts the next piece.
  5. Training backpropagates through the unrolled stacks and rescales any gradient whose norm would exceed 5.0, so a rare very large gradient cannot wreck the update.
  6. For serving, the paper reduces the cost of inference with low-precision arithmetic, because running sixteen LSTM layers for every sentence of an interactive service is expensive.

Why this approach fits

Translation is a sequence-to-sequence problem with a different length on each side, which is the case the recurrent encoder-decoder was designed for. LSTM gating keeps information about the start of a long sentence available when the decoder needs it, and the residual connections let the stack be deep enough to be accurate.

Limitation or tradeoff

Every step depends on the previous one, so neither training nor decoding can be parallelised over time. The paper reports around 6 days to train a basic model on WMT English-to-French with 96 K80 GPUs and describes inference as computationally intensive. The Transformer paper of 2017 names this sequential nature as a limit on parallelism within a training example and proposes a model without recurrence.

What the sources document

  • GNMT uses a deep LSTM network with 8 encoder layers and 8 decoder layers, with attention and residual connections. Only the bottom encoder layer is bidirectional. [13]
  • The paper reports that simple stacked LSTM layers work well up to about 4 layers, barely at 6 and very poorly beyond 8, which it attributes as likely due to exploding and vanishing gradients, and says that residual connections greatly improve gradient flow in the backward pass, which allows very deep encoder and decoder networks to be trained. [13]
  • Training scales gradients down so that their norm is at most 5.0, and uses Adam for the first 60 thousand steps before switching to plain SGD. [13]
  • Google's September 2016 post announces the production launch of GNMT for Chinese to English, with Google Translate's mobile and web apps using it for all machine translations of that pair (about 18 million a day). It describes an encoder that turns the source into vectors and a decoder that writes the output one word at a time with attention, and says neural translation considers the entire input sentence as a unit. The post does not mention LSTMs; the architecture details come from the paper. [14]
  • The Transformer paper states that the inherently sequential nature of recurrent models precludes parallelisation within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths. [15]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 2 of 5

Gboard next-word prediction: a small CIFG recurrent model trained with federated learning

GoogleDocumented in a paper

Hard et al. (2018) describe a recurrent language model for next-word suggestions in the Gboard virtual keyboard, trained on users' phones with federated learning and evaluated in live experiments with a subset of Gboard users. [16]

The problem

A keyboard has to suggest the next word right after each word is typed, without sending what people type to a server, on a phone with little memory. The paper says users expect a visible response within about 20 milliseconds and that on-device language models are usually limited to tens of megabytes. The model also has to be trained on text that stays on the device.

Where this topic fits

The recurrent layer is the language model. It reads the words of the current sentence one at a time, keeps the context in its state, and after each word produces a probability for every word in a 10,000-word vocabulary.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Each typed word is mapped to an id in a 10,000-word vocabulary and looked up in a 96-dimensional embedding table. Special tokens mark the start and end of a sentence and out-of-vocabulary words.
  2. A single CIFG layer with 670 units updates its state with the new word's embedding. CIFG is an LSTM variant that couples the input and forget gates, so one gate controls both how much is written and how much is kept.
  3. In a typical implementation of this design, the layer's output is projected back to 96 dimensions and multiplied by the tied embedding matrix to score all 10,000 words, and the keyboard shows the best-ranked candidates.
  4. For training, phones that are charging, idle and on an unmetered network compute updates on text stored locally, and a server averages the updates (Federated Averaging) into a new shared model.
  5. The trained weights are quantised before shipping, which brings the model on the device to about 1.4 megabytes.

Why this approach fits

Typing is a stream: each new word updates a small state and the model needs no access to the older history afterwards. A one-layer recurrent model with a tied embedding is small enough to ship and to train on a phone, and the CIFG removes a quarter of the gate parameters of an LSTM layer while keeping a gated state to carry the sentence context.

Limitation or tradeoff

The model is deliberately small: a 10,000-word vocabulary, one layer, and context that lasts for one sentence, so it cannot use long-range context. Federated training also depends on enough devices meeting the conditions of free memory, charging, idleness and an unmetered network.

What the sources document

  • The paper trains a recurrent neural network language model for next-word prediction in a virtual keyboard using federated learning, with the Federated Averaging algorithm on client devices. [16]
  • The model is a single-layer CIFG with 670 units, a 96-dimensional input embedding and output projection, a 10,000-word vocabulary and about 1.4 million parameters, more than two thirds of them in the embedding matrix, which is tied between input and output. [16]
  • The CIFG uses a single gate to control both the input and the recurrent cell self-connection, reducing the parameters per cell by 25%, and the paper says this reduces computation and parameter count with no impact on model performance. [16]
  • The paper states that users expect a visible keyboard response within 20 milliseconds, that language models on devices are usually limited to tens of megabytes, and that after weight quantisation the model shipped to Gboard devices is 1.4 megabytes. [16]
  • Clients take part in federated rounds only if they have at least 2 gigabytes of memory available and are charging, on an unmetered network and idle; the paper also reports live experiments with a subset of Gboard users. [16]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 3 of 5

Amazon SageMaker DeepAR: one recurrent forecaster shared across hundreds of related time series

Amazon Web ServicesDocumented in official docs

The built-in DeepAR algorithm of Amazon SageMaker, described in the AWS documentation pages on the DeepAR forecasting algorithm and on how it works, and in the DeepAR paper by Salinas, Flunkert and Gasthaus. It forecasts a time series with a recurrent network that is trained jointly over many related series. [17][18][19]

The problem

A retailer or operator has many similar series, such as demand for different products or load on different servers, some of them short or new. Fitting one ARIMA or ETS model per series wastes the structure the series share and sees only each series' own history. The goal is a probabilistic forecast for every series that borrows patterns, such as weekly cycles or the effect of a promotion, from the others.

Where this topic fits

The recurrent network is the forecasting model. Its hidden state summarises the recent past of one series. At each step it receives the previous value, known covariates and a series embedding, and it outputs the parameters of a probability distribution for the next value.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Each record is a series with a start time, target values, optional categorical features (embedded per group) and optional dynamic features that are known in the future, such as a promotion flag.
  2. SageMaker derives calendar features from the series' frequency (for hourly data, hour of day, day of week and so on) and feeds lagged target values, for example from one, two and three days earlier.
  3. SageMaker randomly samples training examples from each series, and each example is a pair of adjacent windows: a context window of length context_length that conditions the network and a prediction window of length prediction_length that it must forecast.
  4. In the paper's model, one multi-layer LSTM network is unrolled over the context window and then over the prediction window, with the previous target value fed in at each step. At every step it outputs the parameters of a distribution and is trained to give the observed value high likelihood.
  5. In the paper's procedure, the network is run over the observed history at inference, then a sample from its predicted distribution is fed back as the next input, step after step across the horizon. Repeating this gives many sample paths from which a forecast distribution is estimated.

Why this approach fits

One recurrent network with shared weights can be trained on many windows drawn from all series, so a new or short series benefits from what the network learned elsewhere. The hidden state removes the need to choose a lag structure for each series, and sampling gives distributions rather than single point forecasts.

Limitation or tradeoff

AWS says a DeepAR model trained on a single series may be less accurate than ARIMA or ETS and that the advantage appears with hundreds of related series. It also says that prediction_length values above 400 make the model slow and less accurate, and that dynamic features must be known for the whole forecast horizon. Feeding samples back also lets errors accumulate over a long horizon, which is our explanation of why the horizon limit matters.

What the sources document

  • DeepAR is a supervised algorithm for forecasting scalar time series with recurrent neural networks. It trains a single model jointly over many related series instead of fitting one model per series as ARIMA and ETS do. [17]
  • AWS states that DeepAR outperforms the standard ARIMA and ETS methods when the dataset contains hundreds of related time series, and recommends training on as many series as are available. [17]
  • Each training example is a pair of adjacent context and prediction windows of fixed lengths, set by the context_length and prediction_length hyperparameters. Lagged values of the target are fed in automatically, so the model can look back further than context_length. [18]
  • At inference the trained model forecasts a probability distribution for the next prediction_length values. Categorical features are learned as per-group embeddings, and dynamic feature series must be known in the future. [18]
  • The paper computes the hidden state at each step from the previous hidden state, the previous target value and the current covariates, implements this with a multi-layer recurrent network with LSTM cells, and forecasts by sampling a value from the predicted distribution and feeding it back into the recurrence. [19]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 4 of 5

Gboard on-device speech recognition with an RNN transducer built from LSTM networks

GoogleDocumented in an engineering article

The Google Research post 'An All-Neural On-Device Speech Recognizer' (March 2019) describes the dictation model launched for Gboard on Pixel phones: a recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) whose encoder and prediction networks are LSTM networks. [20]

The problem

Dictation must show words as the person speaks rather than after they finish, and it must work without a round trip to a server. Earlier recognisers used separately trained acoustic, pronunciation and language models that were composed into a large search graph, which is hard to fit on a phone.

Where this topic fits

Two recurrent stacks are the model. The encoder reads audio frame by frame with a state that summarises the audio so far. The prediction network is a recurrent language model over the symbols already emitted. A small feed-forward joint network combines the two to choose the next symbol.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Audio is processed continuously. The encoder, a stack of LSTM layers, turns each new piece of audio into an encoding and carries its state forward, so it never needs the whole utterance.
  2. The prediction network, also an LSTM stack, takes the previously emitted symbol and updates its own state, which summarises the text produced so far.
  3. The joint network, a feed-forward network, combines the encoder output with the prediction network output, and a softmax gives probabilities over the output symbols.
  4. Each predicted symbol is fed back into the prediction network, so predictions depend both on the audio heard so far and on what was already output.
  5. The trained model is 450 MB, which the post says is a lot even for today's smartphones. Parameter quantisation and hybrid kernels give a 4x compression relative to the floating-point models and a 4x run-time speedup, and the final model is 80 MB and runs faster than real time on a single core. The post does not reconcile 450 MB with 4x and 80 MB.

Why this approach fits

A recurrent state is what streaming needs: the model keeps a fixed-size summary of the audio heard so far, so the work per new audio frame does not grow with the length of the utterance, and output can be produced continuously. The LSTM prediction network gives the transducer a language model inside the same network, in place of a separate search graph.

Limitation or tradeoff

A streaming encoder can only use audio that has already arrived, unlike a bidirectional model that sees the whole utterance. The post reports a launch limited to American English on Pixel phones, and a final size of 80 MB after quantisation and compression, down from 450 MB as trained. Its statement that the accuracy matches server-based models is Google's own claim, and this lesson reproduces no measured error rates.

What the sources document

  • The post describes RNN-Ts as sequence-to-sequence models without attention that continuously process input samples and stream output symbols, which suits streaming dictation. [20]
  • The prediction and encoder networks are LSTM RNNs and the joint model is feed-forward. Predicted symbols are fed back through the prediction network so that predictions depend on both the audio so far and past outputs. [20]
  • The prediction network has 2 layers of 2048 units with a 640-dimensional projection layer, and the encoder has 8 such layers. [20]
  • The trained RNN-T is 450 MB. Parameter quantisation and hybrid kernels gave a 4x compression with respect to the floating-point models and a 4x run-time speedup, and the final model after compression is 80 MB; the post does not reconcile these figures. [20]
  • The recognizer powers speech input in Gboard and was initially launched to all Pixel phones in American English only. [20]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 5 of 5

OpenAI Five: a 4096-unit LSTM as the memory of a Dota 2 agent

OpenAIDocumented in a paper

The paper 'Dota 2 with Large Scale Deep Reinforcement Learning' (2019) describes the policy network of OpenAI Five, the system that defeated Team OG, the Dota 2 world champions at the time. The core of the network is a single large LSTM. [21]

The problem

Dota 2 is only partly observable: each team sees just the part of the game near its own units and buildings. The right action now may depend on something seen earlier, such as an opponent who walked out of view. A policy that sees only the current observation cannot use that history, so the agent needs a memory that it builds for itself.

Where this topic fits

The LSTM is the core of the policy. At every timestep it takes the processed observation together with its own previous state and produces the state from which the agent's actions are chosen.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. The game engine runs at 30 frames per second, but the agent acts on every 4th frame. Each of those frames is one timestep, roughly 7.5 per second of game time.
  2. At each timestep the agent builds an observation of what its team can currently see.
  3. The observation goes into the LSTM along with the hidden and cell states from the previous timestep, so the new state carries forward what was seen earlier.
  4. The LSTM output is used to choose the next actions, and the new states are kept for the following timestep while the game is played.
  5. For training, the paper uses truncated backpropagation through time over samples of 16 timesteps, and a figure caption says rollout segments are subdivided into such samples. The paper does not describe how the LSTM state at the start of a sample is obtained; a common implementation starts each sample from the state saved during play and passes no gradient back beyond the sample's first step.

Why this approach fits

Partial observability turns a game into a sequence problem: the right action depends on a history, not only on the current frame. An LSTM can learn what to remember from the reward signal alone, without hand-written rules about which past events matter, and its constant cost per step allows acting several times a second.

Limitation or tradeoff

Gradients reach back only 16 timesteps, about two seconds of play at roughly 7.5 timesteps per second, so anything the agent remembers for longer has to be kept alive by the carried state without a gradient that spans that gap. This is our reading of the truncation. The paper also reports about ten months of continual training at a scale of roughly 2 million frames every 2 seconds.

What the sources document

  • The policy network consists primarily of a single-layer 4096-unit LSTM, and the paper describes the network as having approximately 159 million parameters, 84% of them in the LSTM. [21]
  • The paper lists partial observability as a challenge: each team can only see the portion of the game state near its units and buildings, and the rest of the map is hidden. [21]
  • The Dota 2 engine runs at 30 frames per second and OpenAI Five acts only on every 4th frame, which the paper calls a timestep. [21]
  • Training applies the Adam optimizer using truncated backpropagation through time over samples of 16 timesteps. [21]
  • The abstract reports learning from batches of approximately 2 million frames every 2 seconds, continual training over 10 months, and a victory over Team OG, the world champions. [21]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

4Common mistakes

  1. Carrying the hidden state across unrelated sequences, or across batches without detaching it

    Why it causes problems
    Text from one document leaks into the prediction for the next, results depend on batch order, and when the state keeps its history in the autograd graph, memory grows with every batch until training crashes.
    How to recognise it
    Predictions for a sequence change when the batch order changes, or memory use climbs steadily during training.
    How to fix it
    Start each independent sequence from the zero state. When you deliberately carry state across consecutive chunks of one long sequence, detach it (h = h.detach()) at every chunk boundary.

  2. Training a recurrent network without gradient clipping

    Why it causes problems
    One exploding gradient produces a huge update, after which the loss jumps or becomes NaN and the run has to be restarted from a checkpoint.
    How to recognise it
    Sudden loss spikes, NaN losses, or a logged gradient norm that now and then jumps by orders of magnitude above its usual value.
    How to fix it
    Call torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm) after loss.backward() and before optimizer.step(), log the norm it returns, and pick the threshold from the typical norms you see in training.

  3. Using the last output of a padded batch as the sequence summary

    Why it causes problems
    For every sequence shorter than the longest, the last position holds the state after the padding, so the classifier sees a distorted summary and the loss counts padded positions.
    How to recognise it
    Accuracy depends on how much padding a sequence received, or predictions change when the same sequence is batched with longer ones.
    How to fix it
    Pack the sequences with their true lengths, or index each sequence's real last position, and mask padded positions in the loss.

  4. Feeding data in the wrong axis order

    Why it causes problems
    PyTorch's recurrent layers expect (time, batch, features) unless batch_first=True. When the sizes happen to fit, no error is raised, and the network treats the batch axis as time and learns nonsense.
    How to recognise it
    The output has your batch size where the sequence length should be, or accuracy stays near chance even on an easy task.
    How to fix it
    Read the input shape in the documentation or set batch_first=True, and assert the shapes of the input and the output in a unit test.

  5. Expecting an LSTM or GRU to remember across any distance

    Why it causes problems
    Gates are numbers below 1, so a forget gate of 0.9 leaves about 0.5% of the signal after 50 steps. A model that looks fine on short examples quietly fails on the long-range cases you care about.
    How to recognise it
    Accuracy on a test that depends on a token seen n steps earlier falls as n grows, although short-range accuracy is high.
    How to fix it
    Measure accuracy as a function of dependency distance. If it drops inside the span you need, shorten the problem by chunking or summarising, add attention, or move to an attention-based model.

Exercise 1

Measure the gradient that reaches the first input, with and without gates

CodingIntermediateAbout 45 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

Use only Python's standard library, which is free and needs no installation. A one-unit tanh RNN has input weight wx=1.0w_x = 1.0wx​=1.0, recurrent weight whw_hwh​ and no bias. Write a gated additive cell with constant gates, ct=f ct−1+itanh⁡(wxxt)c_t = f\, c_{t-1} + i \tanh(w_x x_t)ct​=fct−1​+itanh(wx​xt​) and L=12(cT−y)2L = \tfrac12 (c_T - y)^2L=21​(cT​−y)2, and print ∣∂L/∂wx∣|\partial L / \partial w_x|∣∂L/∂wx​∣ for the same lengths with i=0.5i = 0.5i=0.5 and f∈{0.95,0.5}f \in \{0.95, 0.5\}f∈{0.95,0.5}.
  5. Write clip_by_norm(grads, max_norm) and try it on [3, 4] and on [0.3, 0.4] with max_norm = 1.0.

Requirements

  • Use only the math module, with no NumPy or PyTorch.
  • Compute the gradient with one backward loop over the time steps, not by finite differences.
  • The BPTT value must agree with the finite-difference value to at least six significant digits.
  • clip_by_norm must return the gradients unchanged when their norm is at most max_norm, and otherwise the vector rescaled to have norm max_norm.

Expected behaviour

For T=10T = 10T=10 and wh=0.5w_h = 0.5wh​=0.5 both methods give about −6.124712×10−4-6.124712 \times 10^{-4}−6.124712×10−4. The magnitudes of ∂L/∂wx\partial L / \partial w_x∂L/∂wx​ are:

TRNN, wh = 0.5RNN, wh = 1.0RNN, wh = 1.5gated, f = 0.95gated, f = 0.5
51.867e-024.113e-026.847e-041.009e-011.150e-02
205.990e-071.028e-025.612e-105.993e-023.605e-07
505.579e-163.201e-034.210e-221.478e-023.357e-16

The plain RNN gradient collapses with length, and a recurrent weight of 1.5 collapses faster than 1.0 because the state saturates. The gated cell keeps a usable gradient when its forget gate is near 1 and loses it just as fast as the RNN when the gate is 0.5. Clipping [3, 4] (norm 5) gives [0.6, 0.8] and leaves [0.3, 0.4] unchanged.

Hint 1

Go backwards from $t = T$ to 1. Start with $\partial L / \partial h_T = h_T - y$, multiply by $1 - h_t^2$ to get $\partial L / \partial a_t$, add $(\partial L / \partial a_t)\, x_t$ to the answer, then multiply by $w_h$ to get $\partial L / \partial h_{t-1}$.

Hint 2

In the gated cell the derivative of $c_T$ with respect to $c_t$ is $f^{T-t}$, and only steps with a non-zero input contribute to the gradient of $w_x$.

Hint 3

Before concluding that a recurrent weight above 1 explodes, print the hidden states for $w_h = 1.5$ and look at the factor $w_h (1 - h_t^2)$.

Show solution

The backward loop mirrors the worked example. The gated cell is a fixed-gate simplification: real LSTM gates depend on the input, so this shows only why a forget gate near 1 helps.

python
import math

Y, WX = 0.9, 1.0

def forward(wx, wh, xs):
    hs = [0.0]
    for x in xs:
        hs.append(math.tanh(wx * x + wh * hs[-1]))
    return hs

def loss(wx, wh, xs):
    return 0.5 * (forward(wx, wh, xs)[-1] - Y) ** 2

def grad_wx(wx, wh, xs):
    hs = forward(wx, wh, xs)
    d_h = hs[-1] - Y                       # dL/dh_T
    total = 0.0
    for t in range(len(xs), 0, -1):
        d_a = d_h * (1 - hs[t] ** 2)       # dL/da_t
        total += d_a * xs[t - 1]           # contribution of step t to dL/dwx
        d_h = d_a * wh                     # dL/dh_(t-1)
    return total

def grad_wx_gated(wx, f, i, xs):
    cs = [0.0]
    for x in xs:
        cs.append(f * cs[-1] + i * math.tanh(wx * x))
    d_c = cs[-1] - Y
    total = 0.0
    for t in range(len(xs), 0, -1):
        total += d_c * i * (1 - math.tanh(wx * xs[t - 1]) ** 2) * xs[t - 1]
        d_c *= f                           # dc_T/dc_(t-1) = f^(T-t+1)
    return total

def clip_by_norm(grads, max_norm):
    norm = math.sqrt(sum(g * g for g in grads))
    if norm <= max_norm:
        return list(grads)
    return [g * max_norm / norm for g in grads]

def seq(T):
    return [1.0] + [0.0] * (T - 1)

eps = 1e-6
fd = (loss(WX + eps, 0.5, seq(10)) - loss(WX - eps, 0.5, seq(10))) / (2 * eps)
print("bptt %.6e  finite difference %.6e" % (grad_wx(WX, 0.5, seq(10)), fd))

for T in (5, 20, 50):
    rnn = ["%.3e" % abs(grad_wx(WX, wh, seq(T))) for wh in (0.5, 1.0, 1.5)]
    gated = ["%.3e" % abs(grad_wx_gated(WX, f, 0.5, seq(T))) for f in (0.95, 0.5)]
    print(T, "rnn", *rnn, "gated", *gated)

print(clip_by_norm([3.0, 4.0], 1.0), clip_by_norm([0.3, 0.4], 1.0))

The program prints:

text
bptt -6.124712e-04  finite difference -6.124712e-04
5 rnn 1.867e-02 4.113e-02 6.847e-04 gated 1.009e-01 1.150e-02
20 rnn 5.990e-07 1.028e-02 5.612e-10 gated 5.993e-02 3.605e-07
50 rnn 5.579e-16 3.201e-03 4.210e-22 gated 1.478e-02 3.357e-16
[0.6, 0.8] [0.3, 0.4]

Reading the table: with wh=0.5w_h = 0.5wh​=0.5 every step multiplies the signal by at most 0.5, so 50 steps leave 10−1610^{-16}10−16. With wh=1.5w_h = 1.5wh​=1.5 the first steps amplify, but the state quickly saturates near 0.86, where 1.5(1−h2)≈0.41.5 (1 - h^2) \approx 0.41.5(1−h2)≈0.4, so the gradient ends up smaller than with wh=1.0w_h = 1.0wh​=1.0. The gated cell with f=0.95f = 0.95f=0.95 keeps 0.9549≈0.080.95^{49} \approx 0.080.9549≈0.08 of the signal over 49 steps, which is why its gradient is still about 10−210^{-2}10−2 at T=50T = 50T=50, while f=0.5f = 0.5f=0.5 behaves like the plain RNN.

Check your answer

  • Does your BPTT gradient match the finite-difference value for T = 10 to at least six significant digits?
  • Does the w_h = 0.5 column fall by roughly a factor of 10^-9 or more between T = 5 and T = 50?
  • Is the w_h = 1.5 gradient at T = 50 smaller than the w_h = 1.0 gradient, and can you explain why using the hidden states?
  • Does clip_by_norm leave [0.3, 0.4] unchanged and turn [3, 4] into [0.6, 0.8]?

Exercise 2

Trace one GRU step, count parameters and choose an architecture

AnalysisBeginnerAbout 35 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

Part A. A one-unit GRU, in PyTorch's convention with all biases zero, reads xt=1.0x_t = 1.0xt​=1.0 with ht−1=0.5h_{t-1} = 0.5ht−1​=0.5. The weights on (xt,ht−1)(x_t, h_{t-1})(xt​,ht−1​) are (0.9,0.2)(0.9, 0.2)(0.9,0.2) for the reset gate, (0.4,0.2)(0.4, 0.2)(0.4,0.2) for the update gate and (0.8,0.5)(0.8, 0.5)(0.8,0.5) for the candidate. Compute rtr_trt​, ztz_tzt​, ntn_tnt​ and hth_tht​ by hand, writing down each pre-activation, then check the result with Python's math module.

Part B. Count the parameters of a single-layer nn.RNN, nn.GRU and nn.LSTM with input_size=10 and hidden_size=20, using the weight shapes in the PyTorch documentation (two bias vectors per weight block).

Part C. For each scenario, name the architecture you would try first, give a two-sentence reason, and say what you would measure to check the choice: (1) predicting the next character of a user's text on a phone with a 2 MB model budget; (2) classifying 30-step sensor windows where the label depends only on the last 5 steps; (3) translating 80-word sentences where the verb at the end depends on the subject at the start, on a GPU cluster.

Requirements

  • Show each gate's pre-activation before applying the sigmoid or tanh.
  • Give the parameter counts as a formula and as numbers.
  • Each scenario answer names one architecture, one reason and one measurable check.

Expected behaviour

The reset pre-activation is 1.0, giving rt=σ(1.0)=0.7311r_t = \sigma(1.0) = 0.7311rt​=σ(1.0)=0.7311. The update pre-activation is 0.5, giving zt=σ(0.5)=0.6225z_t = \sigma(0.5) = 0.6225zt​=σ(0.5)=0.6225. The candidate pre-activation is 0.8+0.7311×(0.5×0.5)=0.98280.8 + 0.7311 \times (0.5 \times 0.5) = 0.98280.8+0.7311×(0.5×0.5)=0.9828, so nt=tanh⁡(0.9828)=0.7543n_t = \tanh(0.9828) = 0.7543nt​=tanh(0.9828)=0.7543. The new state is ht=(1−0.6225)×0.7543+0.6225×0.5=0.2848+0.3112=0.5960h_t = (1 - 0.6225) \times 0.7543 + 0.6225 \times 0.5 = 0.2848 + 0.3112 = 0.5960ht​=(1−0.6225)×0.7543+0.6225×0.5=0.2848+0.3112=0.5960. The parameter counts are 640 for the RNN, 1,920 for the GRU and 2,560 for the LSTM. The scenario answers vary, but each must be justified and testable.

Hint 1

In PyTorch's GRU the reset gate multiplies $W_{hn} h_{t-1} + b_{hn}$, so for one unit the candidate pre-activation is the input term plus $r_t$ times the recurrent term.

Hint 2

One weight block has hidden_size rows. An RNN has one block, a GRU three and an LSTM four.

Hint 3

For scenario 2, compare against a model that has no recurrence at all.

Show solution

Part A and B can be checked with a few lines:

python
import math
sigmoid = lambda v: 1 / (1 + math.exp(-v))
x, h_prev = 1.0, 0.5
r = sigmoid(0.9 * x + 0.2 * h_prev)
z = sigmoid(0.4 * x + 0.2 * h_prev)
n = math.tanh(0.8 * x + r * (0.5 * h_prev))
h = (1 - z) * n + z * h_prev
print(round(r, 4), round(z, 4), round(n, 4), round(h, 4))

def block_params(inp, hid):   # one weight block plus two bias vectors, as in the PyTorch docs
    return hid * inp + hid * hid + 2 * hid

for name, blocks in (("RNN", 1), ("GRU", 3), ("LSTM", 4)):
    print(name, blocks * block_params(10, 20))

The program prints 0.7311 0.6225 0.7543 0.596, then RNN 640, GRU 1920 and LSTM 2560. One block has 20×10+20×20+2×20=64020 \times 10 + 20 \times 20 + 2 \times 20 = 64020×10+20×20+2×20=640 parameters. The GRU uses three blocks and the LSTM four.

Part C, one reasonable set of answers. (1) A single-layer GRU or CIFG-style LSTM with a modest hidden size and tied input and output embeddings, because memory per step is constant and the parameter count is small; the Gboard model in this lesson ships at 1.4 MB. Measure top-3 next-character accuracy against model size and latency on the target phone. (2) A model on the window itself, such as a small 1D convolution or gradient boosting on lag features, because the useful history is only 5 steps; a GRU is the fallback if windows vary in length. Measure it against the recurrent model on held-out windows. (3) An attention-based model, or an LSTM with attention, because the dependency spans about 80 positions and a GPU cluster rewards parallel training. Measure accuracy as a function of the distance between subject and verb, and training throughput.

Check your answer

  • Did you get a reset gate of 0.7311 and an update gate of 0.6225?
  • Does your final h_t equal 0.5960, and does it lie between the old state 0.5 and the candidate 0.7543?
  • Is the GRU count 3/4 of the LSTM count, and the RNN count 1/4 of it?
  • Does every scenario answer include a measurement that could prove it wrong?

6Curated resources

Chosen for accuracy and usefulness, not search rank. Time figures are estimates.

  • Understanding LSTM Networks (opens in a new tab)

    colah's blog (Christopher Olah)

    ArticleBeginnerFreeAbout 30 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    A step-by-step visual walk through the LSTM cell: the cell state as a conveyor belt, each of the three gates with its equation, and the GRU and peephole variants as modifications of the same picture.
    When to use it
    Open it first if the gate equations in this lesson felt dense, or after the worked LSTM step when you want to see the same computation drawn as a diagram.

  • Backpropagation Through Time - Dive into Deep Learning (opens in a new tab)

    Dive into Deep Learning (d2l.ai)

    BookIntermediateFreeAbout 40 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    The derivation of backpropagation through time on the unrolled graph, the full, truncated and randomised truncation strategies, and the matrix-power argument for why gradients vanish or diverge.
    When to use it
    After the worked example, when you want the general derivation and the reasoning behind truncated BPTT.

  • LSTM - PyTorch 2.14 documentation (opens in a new tab)

    PyTorch Foundation

    DocumentationIntermediateFreeAbout 20 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    The exact LSTM equations as implemented, the shapes of every weight and bias, the input and output shapes, bidirectional and multi-layer behaviour, projections and the default zero initial state.
    When to use it
    Whenever you write or debug PyTorch code for a recurrent layer, and to check axis order and parameter counts.

  • On the difficulty of training Recurrent Neural Networks (opens in a new tab)

    arXiv (Pascanu, Mikolov, Bengio)

    PaperAdvancedFreeAbout 1 hour (estimate)

    What it teaches
    The analytical, geometric and dynamical-systems explanation of vanishing and exploding gradients, the gradient norm clipping rule, and synthetic long-range tasks such as the temporal order problem.
    When to use it
    When you need the reasoning behind clipping and want to see how the conditions on the recurrent matrix are derived.

  • The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks (opens in a new tab)

    Andrej Karpathy blog

    ArticleBeginnerFreeAbout 40 minutes (estimate)

    What it teaches
    How the same recurrent cell is used for sequence-output, sequence-input and sequence-to-sequence problems, with character-level language models trained on Shakespeare, Wikipedia, LaTeX and source code.
    When to use it
    For intuition about what a recurrent language model can and cannot generate, before building your own.
